output.intro:
NICo isn't a single program you install on a server. As Chapter 5 showed, it is a set of microservices: `nico-api`, `nico-dhcp`, `nico-pxe`, `nico-dns`, the SSH console and others. They run on a **Kubernetes** cluster of at least three nodes in the datacenter, together with prerequisites such as PostgreSQL, Vault, cert-manager, External Secrets and MetalLB. Almost every install step, health check and troubleshooting command in the NICo docs is a `kubectl` command, so you need to be comfortable with Kubernetes before you deploy NICo.

This chapter covers the parts of Kubernetes the NICo docs rely on. It starts with an idea from networking: the **virtual IP address**, a stable address that belongs to a service rather than to a machine. That idea matters because your DHCP relays and DNS records have to point at NICo before NICo even boots. Then it introduces Kubernetes itself and the objects you will see all the time: Pods, StatefulSets, Jobs, ConfigMaps, Secrets and Services. After that come the extension mechanism, **Custom Resources**, which MetalLB, cert-manager, the Postgres operator and DPF all use. The last four lessons cover Service types, persistent storage, RBAC and Secrets.

Everything here runs on a laptop with `kind` (Kubernetes-in-Docker). You can't run NICo on a laptop, but you can create and inspect the same kinds of objects that NICo's `setup.sh` creates. That way, when the Quick Start tells you to run `kubectl get svc -n nico-system | grep LoadBalancer` and look for `<pending>`, you'll know what you're looking at.

You'll use this chapter right away. Chapter 15 builds MetalLB VIPs and L2/BGP advertisement on top of the Service types covered here. Chapter 17 adds Helm, Kustomize and the Postgres operator. Chapters 19–21 cover cert-manager, Vault and ESO, all of which are built from CRs, Secrets and RBAC.
objectives: Explain why each NICo Core LoadBalancer service needs a fixed virtual IP from the MetalLB pool, and pick valid, unique VIPs from a CIDR range
Create a local Kubernetes cluster with kind and use kubectl to inspect nodes, Pods, StatefulSets, Jobs, ConfigMaps, Secrets and Services
Define a CustomResourceDefinition, create a custom resource and explain what an operator adds
Choose between ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer Services, and diagnose a LoadBalancer stuck in <pending>
Provision durable storage with a StorageClass and PersistentVolumeClaims, and predict the PVC names a StatefulSet creates
Grant a ServiceAccount least-privilege access with a Role and RoleBinding, consume a Secret from a Pod, and check both with kubectl

prequestions.question: Your OOB switches relay every BMC DHCP request to one IP address. NICo's DHCP service runs as a container that Kubernetes might restart on a different server tomorrow. Which IP should the relay point at?
prequestions.answer: An address that belongs to the DHCP service itself, not to any one server: a virtual IP (VIP). Wherever the service runs, it answers on that same address.

prequestions.question: Suppose the address of NICo's API changed every time you reinstalled. What would break?
prequestions.answer: Anything configured ahead of time: DNS records for the API hostname, DHCP relay targets, PXE settings and client configs. The docs warn that random IPs on each install mean these "cannot be pre-configured and will break on redeploy".

lessons.explanation:
In Chapter 3 every IP address sat on an interface of one machine. A **virtual IP address (VIP)** is different. It is assigned to a *service*, and whichever machine is currently running that service answers for it. If that machine dies or the service moves, another machine takes over the same address. Clients notice nothing because they only ever knew the VIP.

This matters a lot for NICo. Its control plane services (`nico-api`, `nico-dhcp`, `nico-dns`, `nico-pxe`, `nico-ssh-console-rs`) run as containers on a Kubernetes cluster of at least three nodes. Kubernetes can reschedule them onto any node. Yet the rest of the datacenter has to reach them at known addresses:

- OOB switches relay BMC DHCP requests to the `nico-dhcp` VIP.
- External DNS must resolve the `nico-api` hostname to the `nico-api` VIP.
- Managed hosts fetch boot artifacts from the `nico-pxe` VIP.

In NICo's reference design, **MetalLB** hands out these VIPs from IP address pools that you define, such as an *internal* pool (`10.180.126.160/28` in the example file) and an *external* pool (`10.180.126.176/28`). The Quick Start is explicit: each NICo Core LoadBalancer service needs a **specific, stable IP** from the pool. Without explicit assignments, MetalLB picks IPs at random on each install, so relays, DNS and PXE can't be configured in advance. Each VIP must fall inside a pool you defined and be unique across services. Services with several replicas that each need their own address, such as the two `nico-dns` instances or the three `nico-ntp` replicas, get one VIP per pod through `perPodAnnotations`.

How does the network learn which node currently holds a VIP? In Layer 2 mode, the holder answers ARP requests for it. In BGP mode, nodes advertise the VIP as a route to the ToR. Chapter 15 covers both. In the reference architecture, MetalLB advertises L3 LoadBalancer VIPs toward the DPU uplinks or ToR switches.
lessons.analogy: A VIP is like a company's main phone number. Whoever is on reception duty picks up, and when they go on break a colleague takes over the line, so callers never need a new number. The analogy breaks down on the switchover: a phone system reroutes the call instantly, but on a network the switches and neighbours have to *learn* the new holder (through gratuitous ARP or a BGP update). Until they do, traffic can briefly go to the old machine.

steps.subgoal: Start a lab container with network namespaces
steps.detail:
Each network namespace acts as a separate machine. All of them plug into one bridge, like hosts on one switch.
```bash
docker run --rm -it --privileged debian:stable-slim bash
# inside the container:
apt-get update && apt-get install -y iproute2 curl python3
ip link add br0 type bridge && ip link set br0 up
for n in client srvA srvB; do
  ip netns add $n
  ip link add v-$n type veth peer name eth0 netns $n
  ip link set v-$n master br0 up
  ip -n $n link set lo up
  ip -n $n link set eth0 up
done
ip -n client addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev eth0
ip -n srvA addr add 10.0.0.11/24 dev eth0
ip -n srvB addr add 10.0.0.12/24 dev eth0
```

steps.subgoal: Run the same service on both servers
steps.detail:
```bash
mkdir -p /srv/a /srv/b
echo 'served by srvA' > /srv/a/index.html
echo 'served by srvB' > /srv/b/index.html
ip netns exec srvA python3 -m http.server 80 -d /srv/a 2>/dev/null &
ip netns exec srvB python3 -m http.server 80 -d /srv/b 2>/dev/null &
```

steps.subgoal: Give the VIP to srvA and use it from the client
steps.detail:
```bash
ip -n srvA addr add 10.0.0.100/24 dev eth0
ip netns exec client curl -s http://10.0.0.100/
# served by srvA
```
The client only knows `10.0.0.100`. It doesn't know srvA's own address, `10.0.0.11`.

steps.subgoal: Fail over: move the VIP to srvB
steps.detail:
```bash
ip -n srvA addr del 10.0.0.100/24 dev eth0
ip -n srvB addr add 10.0.0.100/24 dev eth0
ip -n client neigh flush all   # forget the old MAC for 10.0.0.100
ip netns exec client curl -s http://10.0.0.100/
# served by srvB
```
The client's configuration didn't change. Flushing the neighbour (ARP) table stands in for what MetalLB's L2 mode does in real life: the new holder announces itself with gratuitous ARP (Chapter 15). Run `ip -n client neigh` before and after the move and you'll see the MAC address behind `10.0.0.100` change.
Replace `10.0.0.100` with the `nico-dhcp` VIP and "client" with your OOB switch's DHCP relay. The relay keeps forwarding to one address, and the node behind that address can change at any time.

independentProblem.prompt: A colleague suggests leaving all the VIP annotations out of `nico-core.yaml` and letting MetalLB choose, then updating the switch DHCP relay and DNS after each install. Give two concrete reasons this is a bad idea, and say which addresses you must hand to the network team *before* the first install.
hints: Think about what happens on a reinstall or redeploy, not just the first install.
Which external systems are configured outside Kubernetes and point at NICo services?
The Quick Start names the DHCP relay, DNS records, PXE config and API hostname. Step 6 configures the relay to forward to the nico-dhcp VIP.
independentProblem.answer: (1) MetalLB may pick different IPs on each install, so every redeploy silently breaks the DHCP relay targets, DNS A records, PXE settings and the API hostname until someone notices and fixes them by hand. (2) Those external systems have to be configured in advance. BMCs start sending DHCP requests as soon as they are powered, and the `nico-api` hostname must already resolve to its VIP. Before the first install, give the network team the `nico-dhcp` VIP (relay target), the `nico-api` VIP (DNS A record for the API hostname), the `nico-dns` VIPs, the `nico-pxe` VIP and the SSH console VIP, plus the pool CIDRs so they can route and advertise them.

lessons.selfExplanation: In your own words, explain why a stateless service like `nico-dhcp`, which can run on any node, still needs a stable address that the rest of the datacenter knows about. How does a VIP give it that without pinning it to one machine?

checks.question: Why does the Quick Start ask you to assign each NICo Core LoadBalancer service a specific VIP?
options: MetalLB cannot allocate addresses unless you list them per service
Without explicit VIPs, MetalLB picks IPs randomly on each install, so DHCP relays, DNS and PXE can't be configured in advance
Kubernetes refuses to create a LoadBalancer Service without an IP annotation
A fixed VIP makes the service run faster
checks.answer: Without explicit VIPs, MetalLB picks IPs randomly on each install, so DHCP relays, DNS and PXE can't be configured in advance
checks.explanation: MetalLB can auto-allocate, and the docs say existing configs may omit annotations for automatic allocation. The problem is that the address isn't stable across installs. Kubernetes doesn't require the annotation, and IP choice has no effect on speed.

checks.question: Which statement about a VIP is correct?
options: It is permanently bound to one physical NIC
It belongs to a service, and whichever machine currently holds it answers for it
It is a private address that only works inside a Kubernetes Pod
It replaces the need for each node to have its own IP
checks.answer: It belongs to a service, and whichever machine currently holds it answers for it
checks.explanation: The point of a VIP is that it isn't tied to one machine. Nodes still keep their own IPs. NICo's VIPs are reachable from the underlay, not just inside pods.

checks.question: `nico-dns` runs two replicas, and each needs its own VIP. Which values key do you use instead of `annotations`?
checks.answer: `nico-dns.externalService.perPodAnnotations` (a list: `[0]` and `[1]`)
checks.explanation: The Quick Start says to use `perPodAnnotations` because each replica gets its own VIP. A single `annotations` map would give one address for the whole service.

prequestions.question: You've run containers with `docker run`. What would you need to add yourself to keep 3 copies of a container running across 3 servers, restarting them when a server dies?
prequestions.answer: A scheduler to place containers on servers, health monitoring, automatic restarts and rescheduling, service discovery and stable networking. That is what Kubernetes provides.

prequestions.question: Does NICo install the Kubernetes cluster it runs on?
prequestions.answer: No. Operators provision their own cluster (kubeadm, Kubespray, managed Kubernetes and so on) that meets NICo's requirements: v1.30 or later and at least three schedulable nodes.

lessons.explanation:
**Kubernetes** is a container orchestration platform. You describe the *desired state* ("run 3 copies of this image, reachable on port 443"), and Kubernetes keeps working to make the cluster's *actual state* match. Nodes die, containers crash and images get upgraded, and Kubernetes keeps reconciling. If that sounds like NICo's own design, where API handlers record desired state and state machines drive the hardware toward it (Chapters 4–5), that's because it is the same pattern.

Key terms:

- **Cluster**: a set of machines managed together.
- **Node**: one machine in the cluster. Each node runs a **kubelet** agent and a container runtime such as **containerd**.
- **Control plane**: the components that store desired state and make decisions. The **API server** is the front door, and everything, including you, talks to it.
- **kubectl**: the command-line client for the API server. It reads a **kubeconfig** file (`$KUBECONFIG` or `~/.kube/config`) to find the cluster and your credentials.
- **Namespace**: a named partition of the cluster. NICo uses `nico-system`, `nico-rest`, `temporal`, `postgres`, `metallb-system` and others.
- **CNI**: the plugin that gives pods networking. The validated choice is Calico (Chapter 15).

NICo's requirements: any conformant **Kubernetes v1.30+** (validated on v1.30.4 with containerd 1.7.1 on Ubuntu 24.04), with **at least three schedulable nodes**, meaning Ready and not tainted NoSchedule/NoExecute, for high availability of PostgreSQL and Vault. Every node needs `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` and `net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1`, and must resolve `kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`. NICo does **not** provision the cluster; you bring it. `setup.sh` then runs from your workstation using `kubectl`, `helm` and `helmfile`.

For learning, **kind** runs each Kubernetes "node" as a Docker container on your laptop. It is real Kubernetes with the same API and the same `kubectl`.
lessons.analogy: Kubernetes is like a building's thermostat. You set the temperature you want, and the system keeps switching heating on and off to hold it. You don't flip the boiler yourself. Where it breaks down: a thermostat controls one number, while Kubernetes reconciles thousands of objects of many kinds. It also can't fix a problem it has no way to act on. If an image doesn't exist, it will retry forever and report an error.

workedExample.title: Create a cluster and watch Kubernetes repair itself

steps.detail:
Install Docker (or Podman), `kubectl` and `kind`:
```bash
# macOS
brew install kubectl kind
# Linux (amd64)
curl -Lo kind https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/dl/latest/kind-linux-amd64 && chmod +x kind && sudo mv kind /usr/local/bin/
```
Install `kubectl` on Linux as the Quick Start shows (`snap install kubectl --classic` or the official binary).

```bash
cat > kind-3.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
  - role: worker
  - role: worker
EOF
kind create cluster --name lab --config kind-3.yaml
kubectl get nodes -o wide
```
Wait until all three nodes show `Ready`. `kubectl version` shows the server version, which for NICo must be v1.30 or later.

```bash
kubectl create deployment hello --image=nginx --replicas=3
kubectl get pods -o wide
```
You asked for 3 copies, and the scheduler spreads them across nodes.

steps.subgoal: Break something and watch it reconcile
steps.detail:
```bash
kubectl delete pod $(kubectl get pods -l app=hello -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl get pods -l app=hello
```
A new pod with a different name appears within seconds. Kubernetes saw 2 running where 3 were desired and fixed it.

```bash
kubectl get namespaces
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
```
The cluster's own components (CoreDNS, kube-proxy, the CNI) run as pods too. On a NICo site you'd run `kubectl get pods -n nico-system` the same way.

independentProblem.prompt: You've been given a kubeconfig for a cluster and asked whether it meets NICo's basic Kubernetes requirements. Which `kubectl` commands do you run, and what output do you need to see?
hints: There are two headline requirements: a version and a node count.
One command reports the server version; another lists nodes with their status.
Also check for NoSchedule/NoExecute taints: `kubectl describe nodes | grep -i taint`.
independentProblem.answer: `export KUBECONFIG=/path/to/kubeconfig`, then `kubectl version` (Server Version must be v1.30 or later) and `kubectl get nodes` (at least three nodes with STATUS `Ready`). Then `kubectl describe nodes | grep -i taints` to confirm at least three are schedulable, meaning not tainted NoSchedule/NoExecute. NICo's `preflight.sh` checks the same things and more, including kernel parameters and DNS on each node.

lessons.selfExplanation: Explain why the "declare desired state, let a controller reconcile" model suits running a control plane like NICo's better than a script that starts containers once. Use the example of a node failing at 3 a.m.

checks.question: What is the minimum Kubernetes version NICo supports?
options: Any version, because NICo ships its own Kubernetes
checks.explanation: The docs say "any conformant Kubernetes v1.30+". 1.26 is the minimum *kubectl* client version in the tools table, which is a common mix-up. NICo does not ship or provision Kubernetes.

checks.question: Why does NICo need at least three schedulable nodes?
options: kubectl only works with three or more nodes
For high availability of PostgreSQL and (unless --skip-vault) Vault
Because MetalLB needs exactly three BGP peers
Kubernetes refuses to start with fewer nodes
checks.answer: For high availability of PostgreSQL and (unless --skip-vault) Vault
checks.explanation: The Quick Start ties the three-node minimum to HA PostgreSQL and Vault. Kubernetes runs fine on one node, which is how kind's default works. The number of MetalLB peers depends on your topology.

checks.question: A pod you never deleted has a new name and a recent start time. What most likely happened?
options: A controller replaced it to keep actual state matching desired state
checks.answer: A controller replaced it to keep actual state matching desired state
checks.explanation: Controllers such as Deployments replace pods that crashed or were evicted, and replacement pods get new names (StatefulSet pods are the exception). Kubernetes doesn't rename pods on a timer, and rebuilding an image doesn't touch running pods.

prequestions.question: NICo's built-in NTP service runs three chrony replicas, and each gets its own VIP. Why would a "pick any 3 interchangeable copies" deployment be a poor fit?
prequestions.answer: Each replica needs a stable, distinct identity (name 0, 1, 2) so a specific VIP can stay attached to a specific replica. That is what a StatefulSet provides. Interchangeable copies get random names.

prequestions.question: `setup.sh` registers the site by running a bootstrap task once. What kind of object would you use for "run to completion, then stop"?

lessons.explanation:
Everything in Kubernetes is an **object**: a YAML document with `apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata` (name, namespace, labels) and usually `spec` (desired state). The cluster adds `status` (actual state). You create objects with `kubectl apply -f file.yaml`. These are the ones the NICo docs mention constantly:

- **Pod**: the smallest unit. One or more containers that share a network identity (one pod IP) and can share volumes. Pods are disposable.
- **Deployment**: keeps N interchangeable pod replicas running and handles rolling upgrades. `nico-api` runs as one (`kubectl logs deployment/nico-api`).
- **StatefulSet**: like a Deployment, but each replica has a **stable identity**: names `name-0`, `name-1` and so on, plus its own persistent volume. It is used for replicated stateful apps such as PostgreSQL, Vault, Loki and the site-agent, and for `nico-ntp`, where each of the 3 replicas gets its own VIP.
- **Job**: runs pods until they finish successfully. It is used for one-off tasks such as the site-agent bootstrap Job (`kubectl get jobs -n nico-system`).
- **ConfigMap**: non-sensitive configuration as key/value data or whole files. NICo's site TOML is rendered into the `nico-api` ConfigMap.
- **Secret**: like a ConfigMap but for sensitive data such as passwords, keys and registry credentials. It gets its own lesson later in this chapter.
- **Service**: a stable network name and address in front of a changing set of pods, chosen by **label selector**. Also covered in its own lesson.

Pods pick up ConfigMaps and Secrets as **environment variables** or as **files in a mounted volume**. Labels (`app: nico-api`) are how Services, Deployments and `kubectl -l` find pods. For example, the Quick Start runs `kubectl logs -n nico-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=nico-dhcp`.
lessons.analogy: Think of a restaurant. Pods are the cooks, and you can swap one for another. A Deployment is "always keep three line cooks on shift". A StatefulSet is assigned stations: "station 0 is grill, station 1 is pastry", each with its own fridge (volume). A Job is the caterer hired for one event. ConfigMaps are the recipe book, and Secrets are the safe combination. Where it breaks down: real cooks remember what they were doing, whereas a replaced Pod starts from scratch unless its state is in a volume.

workedExample.title: A ConfigMap, a Job that reads it, and a StatefulSet with stable names

steps.subgoal: Create a ConfigMap holding a TOML file
steps.detail:
```bash
cat > site.toml <<'EOF'
sitename = "mysite"
initial_domain_name = "mysite.example.com"
EOF
kubectl create namespace demo
kubectl -n demo create configmap site-config --from-file=site.toml
kubectl -n demo get configmap site-config -o yaml
```

steps.subgoal: Run a Job that mounts it
steps.detail:
```bash
cat > job.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: read-config
  namespace: demo
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: reader
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "cat /config/site.toml"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: cfg
              mountPath: /config
      volumes:
        - name: cfg
          configMap:
            name: site-config
EOF
kubectl apply -f job.yaml
kubectl -n demo wait --for=condition=complete job/read-config --timeout=120s
kubectl -n demo logs job/read-config
```
The file printed in the logs is the one you put into the ConfigMap. `kubectl get jobs -n demo` shows `COMPLETIONS 1/1`.

steps.subgoal: Create a StatefulSet and note the names
steps.detail:
```bash
cat > sts.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: ntp
  namespace: demo
spec:
  serviceName: ntp
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ntp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ntp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: c
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]
EOF
kubectl apply -f sts.yaml
kubectl -n demo get pods -l app=ntp
```
The pods are `ntp-0`, `ntp-1` and `ntp-2`, created in order.

```bash
kubectl -n demo delete pod ntp-1
kubectl -n demo get pods -l app=ntp
```
The replacement is named `ntp-1` again. Compare that with the Deployment in the previous lesson, where the replacement got a random name. Stable names are what let `perPodAnnotations[1]` keep the same VIP on the same replica.

completionProblem.prompt: Complete this manifest for a one-off database-seeding task that should run once and not be restarted in place when it finishes.
completionProblem.partialSolution:

independentProblem.prompt: For each item, name the object type you'd use and say why: (a) NICo's `site.toml`; (b) the PostgreSQL database password; (c) a 3-node PostgreSQL cluster where each member keeps its own data; (d) the API server, where any replica can serve any request; (e) a stable name other pods use to reach the API.
hints: Split the list into config objects and workload objects.
Ask yourself: is it sensitive? Does it need a stable identity? Does it run to completion?
(c) needs per-replica identity and storage; (d) needs interchangeable replicas; (e) isn't a workload at all.
independentProblem.answer: (a) ConfigMap: non-sensitive configuration, mounted as a file. (b) Secret: sensitive (NICo's DB credentials arrive as Secrets such as `nico-system.nico.nico-pg-cluster.credentials`). (c) StatefulSet: stable names and per-replica volumes. (d) Deployment: interchangeable replicas (`deployment/nico-api`). (e) Service: a stable name and IP in front of pods selected by label.

lessons.selfExplanation: Why does Kubernetes separate configuration (ConfigMaps and Secrets) from workloads (Pods, Deployments, StatefulSets), instead of baking `site.toml` into the container image? Think about how NICo builds one set of images (Chapter 13) and deploys it to many sites.

checks.question: The NICo site-agent bootstrap runs once to register the site and then finishes. Which object fits?
checks.answer: Job
checks.explanation: Jobs run to completion. A Deployment or StatefulSet would restart the task forever after it finished. A ConfigMap holds data and runs nothing.

checks.question: Why is `nico-ntp` a StatefulSet rather than a Deployment?
options: Each replica needs a stable identity so a specific VIP stays attached to it
checks.answer: Each replica needs a stable identity so a specific VIP stays attached to it
checks.explanation: StatefulSet pods keep their names (`-0`, `-1`, `-2`) across restarts, which suits per-pod VIPs. Speed isn't the difference, and both object types run ordinary container images.

checks.question: How does a Service know which pods to send traffic to?
options: By the node the pods run on
checks.answer: By label selector
checks.explanation: Services select pods whose labels match their selector. Pod names change, and nodes and image tags aren't used for selection.

prequestions.question: The Quick Start runs `kubectl get ipaddresspool,bgppeer -n metallb-system`. Plain Kubernetes has no object called IPAddressPool. Where do you think it comes from?
prequestions.answer: MetalLB installs a CustomResourceDefinition that adds these types to the Kubernetes API, and its controller acts on them.

prequestions.question: If you create one of these custom objects but the software that understands it isn't running, what happens?
prequestions.answer: The object is stored and you can `get` it, but nothing acts on it. Nothing in the real world changes, because no operator is reconciling it.

lessons.explanation:
Kubernetes' API can be extended. A **CustomResourceDefinition (CRD)** registers a new object type with a group, a version, a kind and a schema. After that, the API server accepts **Custom Resources (CRs)** of that kind, and you can `kubectl get`, `apply` and `delete` them just like Pods.

A CRD only teaches Kubernetes to *store and validate* the new objects. To make them *do* something you need an **operator** (or controller): a program, usually running as a pod, that watches those CRs and reconciles them into real state. It is the same desired-state loop from the Kubernetes lesson, applied to your own domain.

You'll meet many CRs on a NICo site:

- **MetalLB**: `IPAddressPool`, `BGPPeer`, `BGPAdvertisement`, `L2Advertisement`. The MetalLB controller turns them into VIP allocation and announcements.
- **cert-manager**: `ClusterIssuer` (`site-issuer`, `vault-nico-issuer`) and `Certificate`. cert-manager turns these into real TLS certificates stored in Secrets.
- **External Secrets Operator**: `ClusterSecretStore` and `ExternalSecret`, which copy credentials into Secrets in each namespace.
- **Zalando Postgres Operator**: a postgres cluster CR (`nico-pg-cluster`) that becomes a StatefulSet, Services and credentials.
- **DPF** (Chapter 36): `DPUDeployment`, `DPUFlavor` and `BFB`, which describe how DPUs should be provisioned.

CRDs are cluster-scoped and named `<plural>.<group>` (for example `ipaddresspools.metallb.io`). Each CR is either namespaced or cluster-scoped, depending on what its CRD says. `kubectl get crd` lists every extension installed in a cluster, which is a quick way to see which operators are present.
lessons.analogy: A CRD is like adding a new form type to a government office: "Form DPU-7, fields: model, firmware". Clerks will now accept and file it. The operator is the department that actually processes Form DPU-7. Where it breaks down: a real office would probably reject a form nobody handles, whereas Kubernetes will happily store a CR with no operator. Silent inaction is the real failure mode to watch for.

prequestions.question: NICo's PostgreSQL is only ever used by `nico-api` and other pods in the cluster. Should it be reachable from the datacenter network?
prequestions.answer: No. It is exposed as a ClusterIP Service on port 5432, which is reachable only inside the cluster.

prequestions.question: On a bare-metal cluster with no cloud provider, what do you think a Service of type LoadBalancer shows as its external IP?
prequestions.answer: `<pending>`, until something like MetalLB provides an IP. That is exactly what the Quick Start warns about.

lessons.explanation:
A **Service** gives a stable name and IP to the set of pods matching its selector. Kubernetes DNS makes it resolvable as `<name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`, for example `temporal-frontend.temporal.svc:7233` or `vault.vault.svc:8200`. The Service's **type** decides who can reach it:

- **ClusterIP** (the default): a virtual IP reachable **only inside the cluster**. This suits internal dependencies. The docs expose PostgreSQL as a ClusterIP Service on port `5432`.
- **NodePort**: everything ClusterIP does, plus a port, by default in the 30000–32767 range, opened on **every node's IP**. Traffic to `<any-node-ip>:<nodePort>` reaches the pods. By default `setup.sh` exposes `nico-rest-api` through a NodePort. It's simple, but clients need to know node IPs and a high port.
- **LoadBalancer**: everything NodePort does, plus an **external IP** supplied by a load-balancer implementation. In a public cloud, the cloud provides it. On bare metal nothing provides it by default, so **MetalLB** fills the gap by assigning a VIP from your `IPAddressPool` and advertising it (L2 or BGP, Chapter 15). Without MetalLB, the Quick Start notes, NICo Core services "stay in `<pending>` state and the site is unreachable".

NICo Core's externally needed services (`nico-api`, `nico-dhcp`, `nico-dns`, `nico-pxe`, `nico-ssh-console-rs`) use LoadBalancer, each with a pinned VIP from the first lesson. Contour's Envoy is also a LoadBalancer and takes its IP from the external pool. Some charts let you change `externalService.type` to `NodePort` or `ClusterIP`, and those types don't need VIPs. The DHCPv6 external Service is always LoadBalancer.

To check which addresses were assigned, run `kubectl get svc -n nico-system` and read the `TYPE`, `CLUSTER-IP`, `EXTERNAL-IP` and `PORT(S)` columns.
lessons.analogy: Think of an office building. ClusterIP is an internal extension, so only people inside the building can dial it. NodePort means every entrance has a side door numbered 30080 that leads to the same desk. LoadBalancer is a published street address with a receptionist who routes visitors, and MetalLB is the city office that hands out that address. Where it breaks down: a building has one location, but a Service's pods can be spread across many nodes and move between them.

prequestions.question: A PostgreSQL pod is deleted and recreated on a fresh container filesystem. What happens to the database if nothing else is configured?
prequestions.answer: It's gone. A container's filesystem is ephemeral. Durable data needs a persistent volume that outlives the pod.

prequestions.question: NICo's reference install doesn't need SAN/NAS or Ceph. Where do you think the PostgreSQL and Vault data actually lives?
prequestions.answer: On each node's local NVMe disk, through volumes created by local-path-provisioner.

lessons.explanation:
Pods are disposable, so anything written inside a container disappears when the pod is replaced. Kubernetes separates *asking for* storage from *providing* it:

- **PersistentVolume (PV)**: an actual piece of storage, such as a directory on a node's disk, a cloud disk or a SAN LUN.
- **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)**: a pod's request, for example "10Gi, ReadWriteOnce". Pods mount PVCs, never PVs directly.
- **StorageClass**: a named recipe for creating PVs on demand. When a PVC names a StorageClass, that class's **provisioner** creates a matching PV automatically. This is called *dynamic provisioning*.

**local-path-provisioner** is a simple provisioner that creates each PV as a directory on the local disk of the node where the pod is scheduled. That is fast and needs no shared storage, but the data lives on **one node**. The pod is effectively pinned to that node, and if the node's disk dies, that copy is lost. Applications therefore provide their own redundancy. That is why NICo runs three PostgreSQL instances with three 10Gi `pgdata` PVs, and Vault with three `data-vault` and three `audit-vault` 10GB PVs, "in the absence of a shared storage solution". Loki uses a single 50GB PV.

In NICo's `setup.sh`, **Phase 1** installs local-path-provisioner and its StorageClasses before anything else, because the Postgres and Vault claims depend on it. PostgreSQL's `volumeSize: "10Gi"` in `values.yaml` sets the claim size.

StatefulSets request storage through **volumeClaimTemplates**, which create one PVC per replica named `<template>-<statefulset>-<ordinal>`. A replacement `pg-1` reattaches to its own PVC. By default, deleting a StatefulSet does **not** delete its PVCs, which protects your data. That is why `clean.sh` explicitly removes released PersistentVolumes.

kind ships local-path-provisioner as its default StorageClass, `standard`, so you can try all of this on a laptop.
lessons.analogy: A PVC is a hotel booking ("one double room, two nights"), a PV is the actual room, and the StorageClass is the hotel chain's booking rule ("standard rooms come from this building"). With local-path, your room is in one specific building. Your luggage stays safe while you go out (the pod restarts), but if that building floods, it's gone, and you can't check into a different building and find your luggage there. Where it breaks down: hotels give rooms back at checkout, while a PV's reclaim policy decides whether the data is kept or deleted.

prequestions.question: A pod in `nico-system` makes calls to the Kubernetes API. Whose identity is it using, and who decided what it may do?
prequestions.answer: It uses a ServiceAccount: its own, or `default` if none is set. RBAC Roles and bindings decide which verbs it may use on which resources.

prequestions.question: Should a pod that only needs to read ConfigMaps be able to read Secrets?
prequestions.answer: No. That is least privilege: grant only the verbs and resources it needs.

lessons.explanation:
Every request to the Kubernetes API server is made by an identity. Humans use credentials from their kubeconfig. Pods use a **ServiceAccount**, a namespaced identity that Kubernetes mounts into the pod as a token. If you don't set one, the pod uses the namespace's `default` ServiceAccount. Kubernetes **RBAC** (role-based access control) decides what each identity may do. It is deny-by-default, so anything not granted is refused.

Four object types:

- **Role**: a list of rules within **one namespace**. Each rule names API groups, resources (`pods`, `configmaps`, `secrets` and so on) and **verbs** (`get`, `list`, `watch`, `create`, `update`, `patch`, `delete`).
- **ClusterRole**: the same, but cluster-wide, or for cluster-scoped resources such as nodes and CRDs.
- **RoleBinding**: grants a Role (or a ClusterRole, limited to the binding's namespace) to **subjects**: users, groups or ServiceAccounts.
- **ClusterRoleBinding**: grants a ClusterRole across the whole cluster.

The Role says *what* is allowed, and the binding says *who* gets it. `kubectl auth can-i` lets you test this without writing code:

```bash
kubectl auth can-i list secrets -n demo --as=system:serviceaccount:demo:reader
```

Why this matters for NICo: operators like cert-manager, ESO, MetalLB and the Postgres operator all run under ServiceAccounts with ClusterRoles that let them watch their CRs and write Secrets or Services. Their Helm charts install these for you, and when one is missing you see `forbidden` errors in the operator's logs. ServiceAccount identity also reaches beyond Kubernetes: Vault's **Kubernetes auth** maps ServiceAccounts in `nico-system`, `cert-manager`, `cloud-api`, `cloud-workflow` and `elektra-site-agent` to Vault roles. That is Vault's own policy (Chapter 20), not Kubernetes RBAC, but it relies on the same ServiceAccount tokens. The `--skip-vault` preflight even checks that `nico-api.automountServiceAccountToken` isn't `false`, because nico-api needs its token to request certificates through cert-manager.
lessons.analogy: RBAC works like keycards in an office. The ServiceAccount is the employee badge, the Role is an access profile ("may open supply cupboards on floor 3"), and the RoleBinding links the badge to the profile. Where it breaks down: a keycard opens doors, but RBAC is far more granular. It can allow `get` on a resource while denying `delete`, which no door lock can do.

workedExample.title: Give a ServiceAccount read-only access to ConfigMaps

steps.detail:
```bash
kubectl create namespace rbac-demo
kubectl -n rbac-demo create serviceaccount reader
kubectl auth can-i list configmaps -n rbac-demo --as=system:serviceaccount:rbac-demo:reader
# no
```
By default the new account can do nothing.

```bash
cat > rbac.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: configmap-reader
  namespace: rbac-demo
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: reader-can-read-configmaps
  namespace: rbac-demo
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: reader
    namespace: rbac-demo
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: configmap-reader
EOF
kubectl apply -f rbac.yaml
```
`apiGroups: [""]` means the core API group, where ConfigMaps, Secrets and Pods live.

```bash
SA=system:serviceaccount:rbac-demo:reader
kubectl auth can-i list configmaps -n rbac-demo --as=$SA   # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete configmaps -n rbac-demo --as=$SA # no
kubectl auth can-i list secrets -n rbac-demo --as=$SA      # no
kubectl auth can-i list configmaps -n default --as=$SA     # no (Role is namespaced)
```

```bash
kubectl -n rbac-demo describe rolebinding reader-can-read-configmaps
kubectl auth can-i --list -n rbac-demo --as=system:serviceaccount:rbac-demo:reader
```
When an operator on a NICo site logs `forbidden`, this is how you check what its ServiceAccount is actually allowed to do.

independentProblem.prompt: An in-house monitoring tool runs in namespace `monitor` and needs to list Pods in *every* namespace, including `nico-system` and `nico-rest`, but must not touch Secrets. Which RBAC objects do you create, and how do you prove it works?
hints: "Every namespace" rules out a plain Role and RoleBinding.
You need a cluster-scoped role and a cluster-scoped binding to a ServiceAccount.
Verify with `kubectl auth can-i list pods -A --as=system:serviceaccount:monitor:<name>` and the same command for secrets.
independentProblem.answer: Create a ServiceAccount `pod-lister` in `monitor`, a **ClusterRole** with `apiGroups: [""]`, `resources: ["pods"]`, `verbs: ["get","list","watch"]`, and a **ClusterRoleBinding** that grants it to that ServiceAccount. Verify: `kubectl auth can-i list pods -A --as=system:serviceaccount:monitor:pod-lister` → yes, and `kubectl auth can-i list secrets -n nico-system --as=system:serviceaccount:monitor:pod-lister` → no.

checks.question: A pod spec doesn't set `serviceAccountName`. Which identity does it use for API calls?
options: No identity, so it can't call the API
The identity of whoever ran kubectl apply
checks.answer: The `default` ServiceAccount in its namespace
checks.explanation: Every namespace has a `default` ServiceAccount, and pods use it unless told otherwise. Pods never inherit the permissions of the user who created them.

Yes, if the verbs include list

checks.question: Vault's Kubernetes auth maps NICo ServiceAccounts to Vault roles. Is that Kubernetes RBAC?
options: No, it is Vault's own authorization, which uses the ServiceAccount token as proof of identity
Yes, Vault creates Roles in each namespace
checks.answer: No, it is Vault's own authorization, which uses the ServiceAccount token as proof of identity
checks.explanation: Kubernetes RBAC governs only the Kubernetes API. Vault checks the token and applies its own policies. They are two separate systems that share the same identity.

prequestions.question: `kubectl get secret X -o yaml` shows `password: bmljby1wYXNz`. Is that encrypted?
prequestions.answer: No. It's base64-encoded, and `echo bmljby1wYXNz | base64 -d` prints `nico-pass`. Protection comes from RBAC, and optionally from encryption at rest in etcd, not from the encoding.

prequestions.question: NICo images come from a private registry. How does a node's container runtime learn the registry password when Kubernetes starts a pod?
prequestions.answer: The pod (or its ServiceAccount) references an image pull Secret of type `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` in the same namespace.

lessons.explanation:
A **Secret** is a namespaced object for sensitive data such as passwords, tokens, keys, certificates and registry credentials. It looks like a ConfigMap, but the values under `data` are **base64-encoded** (or you can write plain text under `stringData`). Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. What actually protects a Secret is (a) RBAC, which controls who can `get` Secrets (see the previous lesson), (b) optional encryption at rest in the cluster's datastore, and (c) keeping the values out of Git and shell history.

There are three common ways a pod uses a Secret:

1. **Environment variable** through `secretKeyRef`. NICo's Day 0 guide exposes the credential KEK this way: `NICO_SECRETS_KEK` with `valueFrom.secretKeyRef` naming `nico-secrets-kek` and key `site-kek-1`. The site-agent gets `DB_USER` and `DB_PASSWORD` from the `db-creds` Secret.
2. **Mounted files**: each key becomes a file. TLS certificates are usually consumed this way.
3. **Image pull Secret**: type `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson`, listed under `imagePullSecrets`. The docs ask for an image pull secret (for example `imagepullsecret`) in each namespace that pulls from your registry. `setup.sh` builds one from `REGISTRY_PULL_USERNAME` (default `$oauthtoken`) and `REGISTRY_PULL_SECRET`.

Secrets are **namespace-local**: a pod can only reference Secrets in its own namespace. That's why NICo uses External Secrets Operator to copy `nico-roots` and DB credentials into each NICo namespace, and why an Ingress TLS Secret must live in `nico-rest`. cert-manager also writes the certificates it issues into Secrets.

Here is a habit worth copying from the docs: create Secrets without the value ever touching your shell history, for example
`openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '\n' | kubectl -n nico-system create secret generic nico-secrets-kek --from-file=site-kek-1=/dev/stdin`, and read one key with `-o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d`.
lessons.analogy: A Secret is like a sealed envelope in a locked mailroom. The envelope (base64) only stops people reading it by accident, and the real security is who has a key to the mailroom (RBAC). Where it breaks down: anyone allowed into the mailroom can open every envelope instantly. There is no extra seal, and that's why `get secrets` permission is so sensitive.

workedExample.title: Create, consume and decode a Secret

steps.subgoal: Create a Secret without leaking it to history
steps.detail:
```bash
kubectl create namespace sec-demo
openssl rand -base64 24 | tr -d '\n' | \
  kubectl -n sec-demo create secret generic db-creds \
    --from-literal=DB_USER=nico --from-file=DB_PASSWORD=/dev/stdin
kubectl -n sec-demo get secret db-creds -o yaml
```
The values under `data` look scrambled, but they're only base64.

```bash
kubectl -n sec-demo get secret db-creds -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_USER}' | base64 -d; echo
# nico
```
Anyone with `get secrets` permission can do this.

steps.subgoal: Consume it as env vars and as files
steps.detail:
```bash
cat > sec-pod.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: sec-demo
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: c
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo user=$DB_USER; ls /creds"]
      env:
        - name: DB_USER
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: db-creds
              key: DB_USER
      volumeMounts:
        - name: creds
          mountPath: /creds
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: creds
      secret:
        secretName: db-creds
EOF
kubectl apply -f sec-pod.yaml
sleep 10; kubectl -n sec-demo logs app
# user=nico
# DB_PASSWORD
# DB_USER
```

steps.subgoal: See what happens with a missing Secret
steps.detail: Edit the pod to reference `secretKeyRef.name: no-such-secret`, rename the pod and apply it. `kubectl -n sec-demo get pods` shows `CreateContainerConfigError`. This is the classic symptom of a Secret that ESO hasn't synced yet or that lives in the wrong namespace.

```bash
kubectl -n sec-demo create secret docker-registry imagepullsecret \
  --docker-server=nvcr.io --docker-username='$oauthtoken' --docker-password=dummy-key
kubectl -n sec-demo get secret imagepullsecret -o jsonpath='{.type}'; echo
# kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson
```
Pods reference it with `imagePullSecrets: [{name: imagepullsecret}]`. The `$oauthtoken` username is NGC's API-key convention, as in the Quick Start.

independentProblem.prompt: Pods in a new namespace `nico-rest` fail with `ImagePullBackOff` against your private registry `my-registry.example.com`, even though `nico-system` pulls fine. Explain the likely cause and give the commands to fix and confirm it.
hints: Secrets are scoped to a namespace.
Which Secret type carries registry credentials, and where does the pod reference it?
`kubectl create secret docker-registry ... -n nico-rest`, then add it to `imagePullSecrets` on the pods or patch it onto the namespace's default ServiceAccount.
independentProblem.answer: The image pull Secret exists only in `nico-system`, and pods can't use a Secret from another namespace. Fix: `kubectl -n nico-rest create secret docker-registry imagepullsecret --docker-server=my-registry.example.com --docker-username=<user> --docker-password=<key>`, then reference it through `imagePullSecrets` in the pod spec (usually through chart values), or run `kubectl -n nico-rest patch serviceaccount default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"imagepullsecret"}]}'` and recreate the pods. Confirm with `kubectl -n nico-rest describe pod <pod>` (no more pull errors) and `kubectl -n nico-rest get pods` (Running).

lessons.selfExplanation: If base64 isn't encryption, what actually keeps a Kubernetes Secret secret? Explain how RBAC, namespaces and tools like ESO work together to limit who can read NICo's database credentials.

checks.question: Which statement about Secret `data` values is true?
options: They are base64-encoded, and anyone allowed to get the Secret can decode them
They can only be read by the pod that mounts them
They are hashed and cannot be recovered
checks.answer: They are base64-encoded, and anyone allowed to get the Secret can decode them
checks.explanation: Base64 is reversible and adds no security. Access control comes from RBAC. kubectl doesn't encrypt, and hashing would make the values useless to applications.

checks.question: Why does NICo use ESO to put `nico-roots` and DB credentials into each NICo namespace?
options: Pods can only reference Secrets in their own namespace
Kubernetes limits each namespace to one Secret
ESO encrypts them, which Kubernetes cannot do
checks.answer: Pods can only reference Secrets in their own namespace
checks.explanation: Secrets are namespace-local, so a copy is needed per namespace. Secrets don't expire, there's no per-namespace limit, and ESO's job is syncing, not encrypting.

checks.question: A pod sits in `CreateContainerConfigError` right after deployment. What is a likely Secret-related cause?
options: The Secret it references doesn't exist yet in that namespace, or is missing the requested key
The Secret is too large to mount
checks.answer: The Secret it references doesn't exist yet in that namespace, or is missing the requested key
checks.explanation: A missing Secret or key referenced by env or a volume blocks container creation with this status. A missing image shows as ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull instead.

buildTask.title: A mini "site controller" on kind
buildTask.goal: On a local kind cluster, deploy a small stand-in for a NICo control-plane service. It is a 2-replica StatefulSet that reads a TOML ConfigMap and DB credentials from a Secret, and stores state on PersistentVolumes. You'll expose it as ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer, register a custom resource type, and give a ServiceAccount least-privilege RBAC that a Job checks from inside the cluster.
buildTask.whyItMatters: Most of NICo's install and day-2 checks come down to the objects you'll build here: StatefulSets with PVCs from local-path StorageClasses (PostgreSQL, Vault, site-agent), Secrets consumed through `secretKeyRef` (db-creds, the KEK), ConfigMaps holding site TOML, LoadBalancer Services waiting for MetalLB VIPs, CRs reconciled by operators, and ServiceAccounts with scoped RBAC. Once you've built and broken these on a laptop, the output of `kubectl get pods,svc,pvc,jobs -n nico-system` on a real site will make sense.
setup: Docker (or Podman with `KIND_EXPERIMENTAL_PROVIDER=podman`) on Linux or macOS, with about 4 GB of free RAM
A working directory, for example `mkdir ~/nico-k8s-lab && cd ~/nico-k8s-lab`

steps.detail:
```bash
cat > kind-3.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
  - role: worker
  - role: worker
EOF
kind create cluster --name nico-lab --config kind-3.yaml
kubectl version          # Server Version should be v1.30 or later
kubectl get nodes        # 3 nodes Ready
kubectl get storageclass # 'standard' (local-path) should be the default
```

steps.subgoal: Create the namespace, Secret and ConfigMap
steps.detail:
Create the Secret imperatively so the password never appears in a file:
```bash
kubectl create namespace nico-lab
openssl rand -base64 24 | tr -d '\n' | kubectl -n nico-lab create secret generic db-creds \
  --from-literal=DB_USER=nico --from-file=DB_PASSWORD=/dev/stdin
cat > site.toml <<'EOF'
sitename = "mysite"
initial_domain_name = "mysite.example.com"
EOF
kubectl -n nico-lab create configmap site-config --from-file=site.toml
```

steps.subgoal: Deploy the StatefulSet with persistent storage
steps.detail:
```bash
cat > app.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: fake-api-headless
  namespace: nico-lab
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: fake-api
  ports:
    - port: 8080
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: fake-api
  namespace: nico-lab
spec:
  serviceName: fake-api-headless
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: fake-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: fake-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: python:3.12-slim
          command: ["sh", "-c"]
          args:
            - |
              date >> /data/boots.log
              echo "pod=$(hostname) db_user=$DB_USER" > /data/info.txt
              cp /config/site.toml /data/site.toml
              cd /data && exec python3 -m http.server 8080
          env:
            - name: DB_USER
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-creds
                  key: DB_USER
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: site-config
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        storageClassName: standard
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 100Mi
EOF
kubectl apply -f app.yaml
kubectl -n nico-lab rollout status statefulset/fake-api --timeout=180s
kubectl -n nico-lab get pods,pvc
```
You should see pods `fake-api-0` and `fake-api-1`, and PVCs `data-fake-api-0` and `data-fake-api-1`, all `Bound`.

```bash
cat > svcs.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: fake-api
  namespace: nico-lab
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: fake-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: fake-api-np
  namespace: nico-lab
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: fake-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
      nodePort: 30080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: fake-api-lb
  namespace: nico-lab
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: fake-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
EOF
kubectl apply -f svcs.yaml
kubectl -n nico-lab get svc
```
Note that `fake-api-lb` stays at EXTERNAL-IP `<pending>`. kind has no MetalLB, which is the same symptom the Quick Start warns about for NICo Core.

steps.subgoal: Add least-privilege RBAC and check it from inside a pod
steps.detail:
The Job calls the Kubernetes API directly using its ServiceAccount token:
```bash
cat > rbac.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: config-reader
  namespace: nico-lab
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: configmap-reader
  namespace: nico-lab
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps"]
    verbs: ["get", "list"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: config-reader-binding
  namespace: nico-lab
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: config-reader
    namespace: nico-lab
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: configmap-reader
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: rbac-probe
  namespace: nico-lab
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: config-reader
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: probe
          image: curlimages/curl
          command: ["sh", "-c"]
          args:
            - |
              SA=/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount
              TOKEN=$(cat $SA/token)
              API=https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/nico-lab
              echo "configmaps: $(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --cacert $SA/ca.crt -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $API/configmaps)"
              echo "secrets: $(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --cacert $SA/ca.crt -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $API/secrets)"
EOF
kubectl apply -f rbac.yaml
kubectl -n nico-lab wait --for=condition=complete job/rbac-probe --timeout=120s
kubectl -n nico-lab logs job/rbac-probe
```
Expected output: `configmaps: 200` and `secrets: 403`.

```bash
# Delete a replica: it comes back with the same name and the same volume
kubectl -n nico-lab delete pod fake-api-0
kubectl -n nico-lab wait --for=condition=Ready pod/fake-api-0 --timeout=120s

# Read through the ClusterIP Service (from inside the cluster)
kubectl run tmp -n nico-lab --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- \
  -s http://fake-api-0.fake-api-headless.nico-lab.svc.cluster.local:8080/boots.log

# Read through the NodePort on a node IP
NODE=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[1].status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')
kubectl run tmp2 -n nico-lab --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- \
  -s http://$NODE:30080/site.toml
```
`boots.log` should have **two** timestamps, and the NodePort request should return your TOML.

hints: Pods stuck in `CreateContainerConfigError`: the `db-creds` Secret is missing or was created in a different namespace. Check with `kubectl -n nico-lab get secret db-creds`.

PVCs stuck in `Pending` with no pods yet is normal for `WaitForFirstConsumer`. If they stay Pending after pods are scheduled, check `kubectl get pods -n local-path-storage` and `kubectl describe pvc`.
`kubectl apply -f rack.yaml` says `no matches for kind "Rack"`: the CRD wasn't established yet. Run the `kubectl wait --for=condition=Established` line and apply again.

The rbac-probe Job shows `configmaps: 403`: check that the RoleBinding's subject namespace and name exactly match the ServiceAccount, and that the Job sets `serviceAccountName: config-reader`. Jobs are immutable, so delete it (`kubectl -n nico-lab delete job rbac-probe`) and re-apply.
`kubectl run tmp` fails with `AlreadyExists`: an earlier run left the pod behind. Run `kubectl -n nico-lab delete pod tmp`.
Re-running the Job: Kubernetes won't re-run a completed Job with the same name. Delete it first.
On Podman, run `export KIND_EXPERIMENTAL_PROVIDER=podman` before `kind create cluster`.
buildTask.stretch: Give `fake-api-lb` a real, *pinned* VIP. Install MetalLB in kind (`kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/metallb/metallb/v0.14.5/config/manifests/metallb-native.yaml`, the version NICo validates). Find kind's Docker subnet with `docker network inspect kind`, then create an `IPAddressPool` with a small range from the top of that subnet and an `L2Advertisement` in `metallb-system`. Annotate the Service with `metallb.universe.tf/loadBalancerIPs: <an IP from the pool>` and watch EXTERNAL-IP change from `<pending>` to exactly that address. Delete and recreate the Service and confirm the IP stays the same, which is the reason the first lesson gave for pinning VIPs. On Linux you can `curl http://<VIP>/info.txt` from the host. On macOS the kind network isn't routable from the host, so test from a pod instead. Bonus: switch to two LoadBalancer Services and give each StatefulSet replica its own VIP by selecting on the `statefulset.kubernetes.io/pod-name` label, mimicking `perPodAnnotations` for nico-dns and nico-ntp.
